Chapter 1: The Problem and Its Background

Background of the Study

Creating music has always been a highly human activity. It comes from emotion, real life
experiences, and creative goals [1]. However, Artificial Intelligence is rapidly changing how
people create and listen to music [2]. Modern computer programs can scan millions of songs to
learn complex patterns in rhythm and style. Because of this, they can generate new music
incredibly fast [3]. Systems continue to push the realism of synthetic music through deep
generative architectures [4] and specialized language models [5]. Tools like Suno and Udio
show exactly how powerful this technology is today, using advanced networks to create
complete songs with vocals, lyrics, and instruments across many genres [6]. As these systems
become faster and produce higher audio quality [7], experts predict a massive shift in the music
industry. Artificial Intelligence will serve as a helpful assistant for casual creators. However, fully
automated generation threatens to flood platforms with synthetic songs. In the future, verified
human authenticity will become a highly valued premium commodity.

The results of this shift are urgent and are already causing global backlash. A large
international survey by Deezer and Ipsos found that 97 percent of participants could not tell the
difference between human made and fully Al generated music [8]. Because people cannot hear
the difference, synthetic tracks are flooding streaming platforms. This directly threatens the
income of real musicians. Experts project a 12.7 billion dollar loss for musicians by 2028 [9],
alongside a massive drop in revenue [10]. In response, international artists are becoming
fiercely protective. The Artist Rights Alliance, which represents over 200 massive global artists,
recently released an open letter. They condemned the predatory use of Artificial Intelligence that
devalues human creativity [11]. Without reliable detection technology, the music industry cannot
protect authentic human work or ensure fair pay for artists.

Existing detection tools try to solve this problem, but they are technically weak.
Traditional machine learning methods provide a basic start [12], while newer networks try to find
visual and timing errors in the audio [13], [14]. Despite these efforts, international detection
systems fail in three major ways. First, the most advanced single mix models, like the Deezer
Autoencoder, achieve 99.8 percent accuracy in a controlled lab [15]. However, they completely
fail when the audio pitch is slightly shifted. They only look for software glitches instead of real
human musicality. Second, models like SpecTTTra ignore human biological vocal features. They
ignore natural breathing pauses and vibrato, which are proven signs of an authentic human
singer [16]. Third, systems that use two branches often process the entire blended audio file
without separating the vocals and instruments first. This creates messy data analysis. Finally,
these models fail heavily when tested on unseen AI platforms [17].

The urgency of this problem goes beyond the global industry. It is acutely felt in the
Philippines. The Intellectual Property Office of the Philippines currently does not register Al
generated content for copyright [18]. This leaves human artists with very little legal protection.
National artist sentiments reveal deep frustration. Recently, the OPM community sounded the
alarm when an anonymous AI generated artist topped the Spotify Philippines Viral charts [19].
Filipino musicians argue that unregulated software monetizes local culture without permission
